body.objective: Students will be able to use levels and posture.
body.iCan: I can use levels and posture.
successCriteria: I can use levels to show status and relationships
I can use posture to show character
I can explain how movement communicates meaning
body.hook: Before an actor says a single word, the audience already knows a lot about their character: whether they're confident or nervous, old or young, powerful or afraid. How? Through posture, levels and the way they move through space.

vocabulary.definition: The height of a performer's body on stage: low, medium or high.
The way a person holds their body.
How powerful or important a character seems compared with others.
How an actor uses their whole body to create a character.
A frozen stage picture that tells a story.
The area actors use, including distance between characters.

study.title: Status and Levels
study.question: How do levels and posture show who a character is?
study.passage:
Warm-up, Status walk (8 minutes): Walk around the room. The leader calls out numbers from 1 (very low status: shy, unsure) to 10 (very high status: confident, powerful). Change your posture, pace, eye contact and space with each number.
Activity 1, Levels tableau (10 minutes): In groups of four, create three tableaux using low, medium and high levels:
• A king and his servants
• A team celebrating a win while one player sits injured
• A new student arriving at a busy cafeteria
The audience guesses each character's status and explains the evidence.
Activity 2, Status card scene (15 minutes): In pairs, each person secretly draws a status card (1–10). Improvise a short scene in a setting such as a job interview, a bus stop or a restaurant. Show status only with posture, levels, eye contact and space, not by saying it. The audience guesses each number.
Debrief: Which physical choices showed status most clearly?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Warm up with the status walk
discussion: How did your posture change from status 1 to 10?
In the tableaux, how did levels show relationships?
Which physical clue was easiest for the audience to read?
Can a character change status during a scene? How?
study.product: Choose a character from a story or film and describe how you would show their status through posture, level, eye contact and use of space, with a sketch of a tableau.

examples.title: High status
examples.problem: How might a high-status character stand?
examples.answer: Tall posture, steady eye contact, relaxed and taking up space
examples.explore: What would low status look like?

examples.title: Levels
examples.problem: In "king and servants," who should be highest?
examples.answer: The king, standing or on a raised level, with servants lower
examples.explore: How else could you show the king's power?

examples.title: Space
examples.problem: What does standing far from others suggest?

examples.title: Status change
examples.problem: How could a character's status rise during a scene?
examples.answer: The actor stands taller, slows down and makes eye contact

practice.q: How must status be shown in the card scene?
practice.a: Through posture, levels, eye contact and space, not words.
Closeness shows connection; distance shows separation.

practice.q: Name one setting for the card scene.
practice.a: A job interview (also bus stop, restaurant).

practice.q: Why is showing better than telling on stage?
practice.a: Audiences understand and believe what they see.
A high and low character facing each other suggests a power struggle.

practice.q: How might status differ from a character's job or title?
practice.a: A boss can act low status if nervous; a student can act high status if confident.

practice.q: How could you use physicality for a character very different from you?
practice.a: Observe real people and practise their posture, pace and gestures.

misconceptions: Thinking characters must stay the same status
Telling the audience instead of showing
